analysis.investment_thesis: GSPL passes several of my strictest quantitative filters — P/E of 14.6, P/B of 1.29, and a current price of ₹272 that sits meaningfully below the Graham Number of ~₹371 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS ~₹28.97 × BVPS ~₹211)) — providing a genuine margin of safety in the asset base. However, net profit has fallen 30% from its ₹2,342 Cr peak (FY23) to ₹1,637 Cr (FY25), and I cannot commit capital to a business with deteriorating earning power until that trend reverses.
key_strengths: Fortress balance sheet: Debt/Equity of 0.01 (borrowings of ₹140 Cr against equity of ₹11,941 Cr); interest coverage ~46x — almost no financial risk.
Price below Graham Number: ₹272 vs. computed Graham Number ~₹371; P/B of 1.29 and P/E of 14.6 both within my outer limits.
Consistent cash generation: Operating CF positive all 5 years (₹2,741–3,340 Cr range); regulated gas transmission provides durable, government-backed revenue streams.
key_risks: Declining earning power: Net profit fell from ₹2,342 Cr (FY23) → ₹2,184 Cr (FY24) → ₹1,637 Cr (FY25), a 30% drop in two years — the most serious disqualifier for a Graham investor.

Revenue stagnation with rising capex: Revenue is flat at ~₹17,000–18,000 Cr since FY22, while investing outflows hit ₹2,754 Cr in FY25 — capital being consumed without proportionate growth in earnings.
Quality of earnings declining: Other income surged to ₹350 Cr (FY25) vs. ₹56 Cr finance cost — profit is increasingly supported by non-operating items, not core pipeline transmission margins.
red_flags: EBITDA has contracted for 3 consecutive years: ₹4,116 Cr (FY21) → ₹2,991 Cr (FY25); a 27% decline in core operating surplus.
Operating margin compressed to 10.92% on ₹17,370 Cr revenue — for a regulated pipeline monopoly this is suspiciously thin, suggesting tariff pressure or cost creep.
FCF declining while capex remains elevated: FCF dropped to ₹1,550 Cr (FY24) and recovered only partially to ₹1,765 Cr (FY25); the capex cycle is not yet delivering earnings returns.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
GSPL is one of the rare listed businesses that passes my most mechanical filters simultaneously: P/E below 15, P/B below 1.5, near-zero debt, nine consecutive years of positive earnings, and a price materially below the Graham Number. The balance sheet is exemplary — borrowings of a mere ₹140 Cr against equity of ₹11,941 Cr, and interest coverage exceeding 46 times. For a regulated gas transmission utility with state government backing (promoter at 37.63%), the probability of financial distress is negligible. This is the kind of business where Mr. Market's pessimism may be creating a genuine bargain in the asset base.

Yet I cannot ignore what the income statement is telling me. A Graham investor buys earning power, not just assets, and earning power here is clearly deteriorating. Net profit peaked at ₹2,342 Cr in FY23 and has since fallen to ₹1,637 Cr — a 30% decline in just two years. EBITDA has contracted for five consecutive years. Revenue is essentially flat since FY22. Simultaneously, the company is deploying ₹976–1,278 Cr in annual capex (CWIP at ₹1,134 Cr) with no visible earnings uplift yet. The growing reliance on other income (₹350 Cr in FY25, up from ₹94 Cr in FY16) to pad the bottom line is a further sign that core transmission earnings are under pressure. I will watch from the sidelines until earnings stabilize; the margin of safety in the balance sheet is real, but I require proven earning power — not the memory of it.
